title: Fixed draws within shared subcells reduced one bumblebee richness loss estimate in four tests of 1901-2014 records
abstract: We tested whether fixed record counts make bumblebee richness changes stable to shifts in sampling locations. We used public records for Europe and North America in two disjoint time comparisons within 1901-2014. We kept quarter-degree subcells with at least five records in each period. We compared exact richness expectations from fixed draws in each shared subcell with pooled draws from the same records. Both designs kept all four mean change signs. In 168 European cells, the long-period allocation contrast was +0.188 expected species per cell, with a four-test adjusted interval of +0.052 to +0.345. The other three contrasts were uncertain. The European shift stayed positive at two other bootstrap block sizes, but its interval crossed zero with larger subcells or more draws. Removing unmatched locations gave an opposite shift. All four net-contrast intervals included zero. These selected records do not identify true richness change or a climate effect. The test extends a climate-impact analysis; it fits no environmental exposure. Source records and cell tables stay outside the package. Code, aggregate results, checks and a figure support reproduction.

display.caption: Direct contrasts separate draw allocation from location selection. Bars are approximate four-test adjusted block-bootstrap intervals for each statistic. The net contrasts are all uncertain.
